title: Which is greater, (a − b)² or (b − a)²?
description: The board expands a minus b all squared and b minus a all squared with the same expansion, and both come out as the same three terms. A check with seven and two gives twenty five both times. The video breaks the guess that swapping the order changes the square.
teaching_notes: One idea: a number and its opposite have the same square, so the two squares are equal. Watch for students who think that the order of the subtraction changes which square is greater.

source: Figure it Out (squares and patterns, question 1)
video_script.why: The child can expand a take away squared, but has not yet compared the two orders of the subtraction.
video_script.substitution: Expand both squares by the same rule, as the example in the book expanded its squares, and compare the results.
video_script.anchor: the two squares of the book's question, with the numbers eigh and b
video_script.payoff_line: Neither is greater, they are always equal.

final_answer.spoken: neither is greater, they are always equal

maths_rules: (b − a)² = b² − 2ba + a² = a² − 2ab + b², since ba = ab
b − a = −(a − b), and a number and its opposite have the same square
video_script.design: One idea: expand both squares with one rule and see the same three terms. The two squares stay side by side on the board.

narration: <bookmark mark='second'/>Step two, expand the second square by the same rule, with b first. We get b squared minus two b eigh plus eigh squared.
<bookmark mark='swap'/>B eigh is the same as eigh b. The terms then reorder to eigh squared minus two eigh b plus b squared.

beats.on_screen: b − a = −(a − b); a number and its opposite have the same square

marks.same: the note that a number and its opposite have the same square appears

narration: <bookmark mark='opp'/>Step three, see the reason. B minus eigh is the opposite of eigh minus b.
<bookmark mark='same'/>A number and its opposite have the same square, because a negative times a negative is a positive.
<bookmark mark='first'/>Step four, put the answer back in the question. Take eigh as seven and b as two. Seven minus two is five, and five squared is twenty five.
<bookmark mark='second'/>Two minus seven is minus five, and minus five all squared is also twenty five.

beats.on_screen: Answer: neither is greater, they are always equal
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Neither is greater, they are always equal.
